summary:
Saint Petersburg stands under the Russian national framework, which the national record carries. The city's own regional ban on "homosexual propaganda directed toward minors", enacted in 2012, was repealed in 2014, so no separate city-level statute remains in force; the federal statute is the instrument a visitor here is exposed to.

The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) names Moscow and Saint Petersburg as the large urban centres where survey data suggests LGBT+ people feel more able to be open, and where relocation within Russia may be a reasonable option.

A 2023 survey by Coming Out and the Sphere Foundation found 57% of Saint Petersburg respondents out to most friends, 19% out to most relatives and 24% out to classmates or colleagues.

An August 2024 study by Citizens' Watch and the Sphere Foundation on enforcement of the propaganda articles drew 13% of its respondents from Saint Petersburg.
tangentialFactors:
Saint Petersburg is where the statute a visitor stands under began. Vitaly Milonov, a member of the Saint Petersburg Legislative Assembly from 2007 to 2016, was the principal sponsor of the city's 2012 ban on "homosexual propaganda directed toward minors", the measure covered by a New York Times report on 29 February 2012. He said he intended to catch Madonna offending under it during her visit to the city, stated in 2013 that gay athletes could be arrested at the 2014 Sochi Winter Olympics for promoting homosexuality to minors, and protested the Side by Side LGBT film festival in the city in November 2013.

The Home Office note's survey comparison places Moscow at 50% out to most friends, 15% out to most relatives and 19% out to classmates or colleagues, against Saint Petersburg's 57%, 19% and 24%. The two cities are the only ones the note names as places where relocation may be reasonable.
localsOnly: Two Saint Petersburg policewomen were dismissed after being accused of flirting on social media, a case the Home Office note records as evidence of the consequences of visible same-sex conduct for people employed by the state.
outOfScopeNotes:
The Home Office assessment that relocation to Moscow or Saint Petersburg may be "reasonable" is a standard applied to asylum claims, not a finding that the city is safe for trans visitors; how that standard is applied in individual cases is unresolved.

No city-level figures for trans-specific violence, hate-crime recording or prosecutions in Saint Petersburg were identified in the sources reviewed. The survey and study figures above rest on self-selected samples and are not representative of the city's LGBT+ population.

The Human Rights Watch report of 30 June 2025 on extremism-designation convictions carries no Saint Petersburg enforcement data; its only reference to the city is a photo caption for a 2019 Pride rally.
